source.title: Taming Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
source.authors: Gao-Tang Li; Yuzhong Chen; Hanghang Tong

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper investigates a related superposition phenomenon in language models: attention heads can contribute to both contextual and parametric knowledge. It does not test the sparse-feature, dimensionality, or geometric claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports causal knock-out analyses and a simplified theoretical construction concerning contextual/parametric knowledge superposition; these are recorded as findings related to the claim subject, with versions set to none. The J U ICE performance results and hyperparameter values are not rows because they assess the proposed intervention, not the representation claim. The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition but reports no results from that cited work.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the word 'superposition' for attention heads that promote both contextual and parametric answers depending on input. It measures ablation effects on output probabilities, not features stored as overlapping directions. It also does not measure neuron polysemanticity, capacity, SAE features or feature dimensionality. Its theory uses near-orthogonal random embeddings as an assumption and does not test it. This is a related but different construct (head-level functional multi-role), so it belongs under fits_no_version, not a test of any version. The reader's T3 or 'tests' is not justified.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that influential attention heads carry contextual and parametric knowledge in 'superposition', with input-dependent roles. They propose JUICE, a dual-run test-time intervention, which reaches state-of-the-art steering across 11 datasets and 6 models. A simplified two-layer theory explains both the phenomenon and why JUICE works.
record.recipe_differences: The original Toy Models of Superposition studies toy networks representing sparse features under dimensional constraints. This paper instead uses component ablations and a theoretical two-layer attention model to study competing factual-recall and induction tasks; it does not measure sparse-feature geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that component effects vary across clean, substitution, and coherent conflict inputs. It also reports that combinations of individually effective interventions can counteract one another.

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-ablating top 'memory heads' in Gemma-2b raises context probability under substitution conflict. Two of the four heads (9,3) and (13,5) lower it under coherent conflict (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention heads in LLMs are not exclusively 'memory' or 'context' heads; their role in parametric vs. contextual recall depends on input conflict type.

fits_no_version.finding: Combining individually helpful head knock-outs is non-additive. Target probability goes from 0.03 (none) to 0.24 (Top 3) but only 0.14 (Top 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiple individually effective component interventions can counteract each other.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory: a two-layer attention-only transformer trained by gradient descent forms a second-layer head that superposes factual-recall and induction associations. The relative coefficients decide which answer wins under conflict (Prop. 5.2–5.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on distinct tasks yields attention heads that jointly implement both tasks, producing knowledge conflicts at inference.

record.problems: The empirical component analysis in Section 3 is mainly demonstrated with Gemma and the World Capital dataset. It measures effects on output probabilities rather than feature overlap, sparsity, capacity, or geometry. Figure 3 uncertainty is displayed as shaded standard deviations, but exact plotted values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Results in Tables 3–7 and the main intervention comparisons are excluded because they evaluate J U ICE or baselines rather than measuring the representation phenomenon.

untested.parts: No toy-model sparse features exceeding dimensions, no sparsity transition, no geometry measurement; near-orthogonality is only an assumption of the theory.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity-competition measurement.
Head multi-role behaviour arises from overlapping training tasks, but the paper does not frame or measure it as neuron polysemanticity versus superposition.
No measurement of features spread across neurons, and no dictionary or SAE.

record.verdict_notes: The term 'superposition' is used in a different sense from the Toy Models claim. The paper cites Elhage et al. 2022 only for background on polysemanticity. Rows are correctly set to versions none. The JUICE performance tables are rightly excluded as method evaluation.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse features exceeding dimensions, near-orthogonal feature directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity or a capacity account in which important features receive dedicated dimensions and others share.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for other reasons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Does not measure features spread across neurons or identify sparse features using a dictionary or SAE.
Does not evaluate whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not measure whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: Appendix A discusses prior superposition work, but the paper's contextual-parametric superposition construct does not test the catalog's claim versions.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure input-dependent attention-head roles and intervention effects on answer probabilities. The theory models conflicting tasks within attention heads. Neither tests nor uses the representational claims in V1–V6.

source_check.notes: Appendix D.1 specifies filtered World Capital samples: heads are ranked on a small subset and combined ablations evaluated on the remaining samples. These results concern parametric-answer probabilities under coherent conflict, rather than overlapping feature directions.
